cands.bio: Engineer and former State Department Foreign Affairs Officer. He worked at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, then joined State in 2021 through an AAAS Science and Technology Policy Fellowship. Grew up in Amador County. Democratic candidate for California's 5th District in 2026. Has not held elected office.

endorsements.text: Democratic Party of California, California Federation of Labor Unions (AFL-CIO) and California Teachers Association, per Ballotpedia's endorsement list.

In his survey he also lists North Valley Labor Federation, California Young Democrats, several Indivisible chapters, Tuolumne County Supervisor Jaron Brandon, Sonora Mayor Ann Segerstrom and Modesto City Council members Chris Ricci and Eric Alvarez.

cands.gaps: We found no documented statements or actions by Masuda on data centers, development or land use, homestead property taxes, foreign or institutional ownership of homes and land, H-1B or immigration enforcement, policing, gun laws, abortion or school choice. The sources give no year for when his family moved to Amador County. We found no news coverage of controversies or foreign ties. His only career details come from his own campaign site and Ballotpedia survey, and we did not find independent confirmation of them.

cands.bio: Republican U.S. representative for California's 5th District since 2009. Earlier served in the California Assembly (1982–1992, 1996–2000) and State Senate (2000–2008). Worked as a journalist, policy analyst, state senator's chief of staff, and think-tank policy center director. UCLA political science graduate.

controversies.text: Federal records show $22,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $11,234 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26.
Missed 22 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (3.3%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 15, 2026-01-21 to 2026-01-22.

In 2008, rival Doug Ose attacked McClintock for collecting hundreds of thousands of dollars in tax-free per diem ($170 a day) as a state senator, while his family lived year-round in Elk Grove. McClintock said he was entitled because his legal residence was his mother's Thousand Oaks home, and rejected the charge that he was gaming the system.

In December 2020, McClintock joined other House Republicans in a Supreme Court brief backing a Texas suit challenging the 2020 results in other states. The Court rejected that challenge. Before January 6, 2021, he and six colleagues signed a letter saying Congress had no authority to influence the outcome, and he voted to certify.

endorsements.text: 2026 endorsements listed by Ballotpedia include President Donald Trump, the Republican Party of California and the San Joaquin County Republican Party.

cands.gaps: We could not find any documented stance or action by McClintock on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buying, growth limits, abortion, gun laws, school choice or teacher pay, or police pay and pensions in the pages we could read. We found no pledge from him to refuse big-donor or foreign-linked money. The Wikipedia page was cut off in its immigration section, so we left out his H-1B and high-skill visa votes. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey for 2026, so no questionnaire answers are available. Ballotpedia gives two different years for his UCLA degree (1978 in the text, 1988 in the summary box); Wikipedia says 1978.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.
